name: Batmobile
summary: Batman's signature car has been a red sedan, a finned roadster, a TV-show showpiece and a tank-like brute. Every era rebuilds it, yet a court has ruled it is still one recognisable character.

parts.label: Body shell
parts.fact: In the comics the car was first called the Batmobile in Detective Comics #48 (1941); a month later Batman #5 stretched it into a sleek shape topped by a tall, scalloped fin.

parts.label: Engine
parts.fact: On TV, the 1966 car's original drivetrain was pulled out partway through the first season and swapped for engine and transmission parts from a Ford Galaxie.

parts.label: Front end
parts.fact: On film, the Tumbler from Batman Begins (2005) has no front axle at all: each front wheel hangs off its own side arm, a layout that lets the nose rear up under hard acceleration.

parts.label: Cockpit
parts.fact: The 1966 TV car's open twin-bubble cockpit came from the Lincoln Futura, a show car hand-built by Ghia in Turin in 1954 and unveiled at the 1955 Chicago Auto Show.

parts.label: Wheels & chassis
parts.fact: The 1989 film car hid a Chevrolet Impala chassis under its long black body. Two were built by the effects crew at Pinewood Studios in England.

parts.label: Rear thrust
parts.fact: On film, the 1989 car carried a jet turbine with an afterburner at the tail, and its rear styling echoes the Fiat Turbina, a gas-turbine concept car from the 1950s.

trivia: George Barris got the Futura concept from Ford for a token one dollar, then his shop turned it into the TV Batmobile in roughly three weeks.
In DC Comics v. Towle (2015) a US federal appeals court held that the Batmobile is a copyrightable character, so a builder selling replica cars was infringing.
Batman's very first car, in Detective Comics #27 (1939), was a plain red sedan that the story never calls the Batmobile.
The Tumbler began as a kitbash: designer Nathan Crowley glued together pieces of scale model kits, including a Lamborghini Countach and a Hummer.
